learn.hook: The chance of rain today is 30%. But if dark clouds are already rolling in over Mumbai, that chance jumps. New information changes probability: that is conditional probability.
points: Recall: for equally likely outcomes, P(E) = n(E)/n(S); in general 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1 and P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F) − P(E ∩ F).
Conditional probability of E given F: P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F), provided P(F) ≠ 0.
For equally likely outcomes, P(E|F) = n(E ∩ F)/n(F): F becomes the new, reduced sample space.
P(E|F) and P(F|E) are generally different.
Read 'given that', 'if it is known that' as the condition F.

example.q: A fair die is thrown. Find the probability that it shows 4, given that the number is even.
steps: F = even = {2, 4, 6}, so the reduced sample space has 3 outcomes.

learn.reallife: Doctors read test results using conditional probability: the chance of a disease given a positive result is very different from the chance of a positive result given the disease.

items.q: Two coins: P(both heads | first is head)

games.title: Find P(E|F) by reducing the sample space
items: List the outcomes in E ∩ F

quiz.q: P(E) = 0.6, P(F) = 0.3 and P(E ∩ F) = 0.2. What is P(E|F)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by P(E) instead of P(F)

quiz.q: For the same data, what is P(F|E)?
quiz.explain: P(F|E) = 0.2/0.6 = 1/3, which differs from P(E|F).

quiz.q: A family has two children. Given that at least one is a boy, what is the probability that both are boys?
quiz.explain: Given set: {BB, BG, GB}. Only BB works: 1/3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that BG and GB are different outcomes

quiz.q: A family has two children. Given that the elder is a boy, what is the probability that both are boys?
quiz.explain: Given set: {BB, BG}. Only BB: 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Treats it like the 'at least one boy' problem

quiz.q: A coin is tossed three times. Find P(at least two heads | first toss is a head).
quiz.explain: F = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT}. E ∩ F = {HHH, HHT, HTH}. P = 3/4.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full sample space of 8 outcomes

quiz.q: Two dice are thrown. Given that the first die shows 5, what is the probability that the sum is at least 10?
quiz.explain: Second die must be 5 or 6: 2 out of 6.
quiz.mistake: Counts outcomes in the full 36-outcome space

quiz.q: Why must P(F) ≠ 0 in P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F)?
options: We cannot condition on an impossible event, and we cannot divide by zero
Because P(E) must be positive
Because E and F are independent
Because probabilities must be fractions
quiz.explain: If F cannot happen, 'given F' makes no sense, and the formula would divide by zero.
steps: P(E|F) is the chance of E when F is known to have happened
If P(F) = 0, F cannot happen, so 'given F' has no meaning
Also the formula P(E ∩ F)/P(F) would divide by 0
Answer: We cannot condition on an impossible event, and we cannot divide by zero
quiz.mistake: Thinks the condition is on P(E)

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For a die, P(number is 2 | number is even) = 1/3.
Reason (R): Given F, the sample space reduces to the outcomes of F.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Reduced space {2, 4, 6} has 3 outcomes, one of which is 2. R explains A.
steps: R: given F, the sample space reduces to F — true
F = even = {2, 4, 6}, 3 outcomes; E ∩ F = {2}, 1 outcome
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Uses 1/6 from the full sample space

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does P(E|F) mean, and how do I calculate it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! P(E|F) is the chance of E once F is known: P(E ∩ F)/P(F), like shrinking the sample space to F!
teach.nudge: What do you divide by, and why?

revise.summary: P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F) is the probability of E when F is known to have happened, with P(F) ≠ 0. For equally likely outcomes, F becomes the new sample space.
focus: Compute P(E|F) from given probabilities
Use the reduced sample space for dice, coins and families
Tell P(E|F) from P(F|E)
traps: Divide by P(F), the given event, not by P(E)
'At least one boy' and 'elder is a boy' give different reduced spaces
Don't use the full sample space after conditioning

learn.hook: Conditional probability is a full probability in its own right: it obeys the same rules, just inside the smaller world F.
points: P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) − P((A ∩ B)|F); if A and B are disjoint, the last term is 0.
Typical settings: dice, coins, cards and families with children.
With cards, remember: 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 4 aces/kings/queens/jacks, 26 red and 26 black, 12 face cards.

example.q: A card is drawn from a pack of 52. Given that it is red, find the probability that it is a king.

learn.reallife: Cricket statisticians quote 'probability of winning given the team bats first'. Its complement, the probability of not winning given batting first, is 1 minus that value.

games.title: Property check
items: Given F has happened, F is certain.
Complements work inside the reduced space.
The complement rule is P(E|F) + P(E′|F) = 1, not this.
If A and B are disjoint, P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F).

quiz.q: If P(E|F) = 0.4, what is P(E′|F)?
quiz.mistake: Thinks the complement rule does not apply to conditional probability

quiz.q: P(A|F) = 0.5, P(B|F) = 0.3 and P((A ∩ B)|F) = 0.1. What is P((A ∪ B)|F)?
A card is drawn from a pack of 52. Given that it is a face card, what is the probability that it is a queen?
quiz.explain: There are 12 face cards, 4 of them queens: 4/12 = 1/3.

quiz.q: Two dice are thrown. Given that a doublet appears, what is the probability that the sum is 6?
quiz.explain: Doublets: 6 outcomes. Sum 6 among them: (3, 3) only. 1/6.
quiz.mistake: Counts all ways to get sum 6 (5 ways)

quiz.q: What is P(S|F) for any event F with P(F) ≠ 0?
options: P(F)
P(S)P(F)
steps: S ∩ F = F, so P(S|F) = P(F)/P(F)

quiz.q: A die is rolled. E = {1, 3, 5}, F = {1, 2, 3}. What is P(E′|F)?
quiz.mistake: Gives P(E|F) instead of its complement

quiz.q: A coin is tossed twice. Given that at least one tail appears, what is the probability of exactly one head?
quiz.explain: Given set {HT, TH, TT}; exactly one head: HT, TH. 2/3.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): P(E|F) + P(E′|F) = 1.
Reason (R): E and E′ are disjoint and together make up the whole sample space.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: Using the union rule for disjoint events, P((E ∪ E′)|F) = P(S|F) = 1, which gives A.
steps: R: E ∩ E′ = φ and E ∪ E′ = S — true
So P(E|F) + P(E′|F) = P((E ∪ E′)|F) = P(S|F) = 1
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Do the usual probability rules still work for conditional probability?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Yes! Complements, unions and P(F|F) = 1 all work inside the reduced space F. Same rules, smaller world!
teach.nudge: What is P(E′|F) in terms of P(E|F)?

revise.summary: Conditional probability follows the usual rules within F: P(S|F) = 1, the union rule, and P(E′|F) = 1 − P(E|F).
focus: Use the complement and union rules for conditional probability
Solve card, dice and coin problems with a condition
remember: P((A ∪ B)|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) − P((A ∩ B)|F)
Pack: 52 cards, 13 per suit, 12 face cards, 26 red
traps: Subtract the intersection in the union rule
Use 12 face cards, not 52, when the card is known to be a face card
Don't give P(E|F) when its complement is asked

learn.hook: Draw two cards one after the other without putting the first back. The second draw depends on the first, and the multiplication theorem handles that chain.
points: P(E ∩ F) = P(E) P(F|E) = P(F) P(E|F), for P(E), P(F) ≠ 0.
For three events: P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E) P(F|E) P(G|E ∩ F).
Without replacement, the counts change after each draw: numerator and denominator both drop.
Read problems in order: first draw, then second given the first, and so on.
Sanity check: the answer can never be larger than any single probability in the chain.

example.q: An urn has 10 black and 5 white balls. Two are drawn one after the other without replacement. Find P(both black).

learn.reallife: Quality inspectors pick parts without replacement from a lot; the multiplication theorem gives the chance that every part in the sample passes.

games.title: Three cards without replacement: king, king, ace

items.q: Bag 4 white, 6 black: P(white, then black)

quiz.q: An urn has 10 black and 5 white balls. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(both black)?
quiz.mistake: Uses 10/15 twice, as if with replacement

quiz.q: A box has 5 red, 3 white and 2 blue balls. Three are drawn one after another without replacement. What is P(red, then white, then blue)?
quiz.mistake: Keeps the denominator 10 for every draw, getting 3/100

quiz.q: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(first red, second blue)?
P(E) = 0.5 and P(F|E) = 0.4. What is P(E ∩ F)?
A box has 4 defective and 16 good bulbs. Two are taken without replacement. What is P(both defective)?
Two cards are drawn without replacement from 52. What is P(both are hearts)?
quiz.mistake: Stops after the first draw and gives 1/4

quiz.q: Which formula gives P(E ∩ F ∩ G)?
options: P(E) P(F|E) P(G|E ∩ F)
P(E) P(F) P(G) always
P(E|F) P(F|G) P(G|E)
P(E) + P(F) + P(G)
quiz.explain: The multiplication theorem extends step by step, each factor conditioned on everything before it.
steps: Multiplication theorem, one event at a time
P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E) × P(F|E) × P(G|E ∩ F)
Each factor is conditioned on everything before it; P(E)P(F)P(G) needs independence

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): When drawing two balls without replacement, P(second red | first red) is less than P(first red) if the bag has both colours.
Reason (R): After removing a red ball, the proportion of red balls in the bag decreases.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With r red out of n (r < n), (r − 1)/(n − 1) < r/n. R explains why.
steps: With r red in n balls (0 < r < n): P(first red) = r/n
P(second red | first red) = (r − 1)/(n − 1), and (r − 1)/(n − 1) < r/n since r < n
R: removing a red ball lowers the red proportion — that is the reason
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the second probability stays the same

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the chance that two things happen one after another?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Multiply P(first) by P(second given first), updating the counts if nothing is replaced!
teach.nudge: What changes in the second fraction when you do not replace?

revise.summary: P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F|E), and for three events P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F|E)P(G|E ∩ F). Without replacement, the counts change after each draw.
focus: Find probabilities of successive draws without replacement
Use P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F|E)
Extend to three events
remember: Without replacement: reduce both numerator and denominator
traps: Don't keep the same denominator on later draws
Multiply, don't add, for 'and'
Don't assume independence unless told

learn.hook: Tossing a coin in Delhi does not change a die roll in Chennai. Such events are independent: knowing one tells you nothing about the other.
points: E and F are independent if P(E|F) = P(E) (with P(F) ≠ 0), equivalently P(E ∩ F) = P(E) P(F).
Independent is NOT the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive means P(E ∩ F) = 0.
Two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.
E, F, G are mutually independent if P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), P(F ∩ G) = P(F)P(G), P(E ∩ G) = P(E)P(G) and P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F)P(G).
Pairwise independence alone does not guarantee mutual independence.

example.q: A die is thrown. E = multiple of 3, F = even number. Are E and F independent?
example.answer: Yes, E and F are independent.

learn.reallife: Safety systems often use independent backups: if each fails rarely and independently, the chance of all failing together is the product of the small chances, which is tiny.

games.title: Independent or mutually exclusive?
items: First toss head; second toss head
Card is a king; same card is a queen
Student passes; same student fails the same exam

games.title: Independence facts
items: If P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), A and B are independent.
Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are independent.
Pairwise independence of three events implies mutual independence.
The triple product condition is also needed.
Successive tosses of a fair coin are independent.
One toss does not affect another.
The bag is restored each time.

quiz.q: A and B are independent with P(A) = 1/2 and P(B) = 1/3. What is P(A ∩ B)?
quiz.explain: Independence gives P(A ∩ B) = (1/2)(1/3) = 1/6.

quiz.q: With the same independent A and B (P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3), what is P(A ∪ B)?
P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4 and A, B are independent. What is P(A ∪ B)?
quiz.mistake: Treats A and B as mutually exclusive

quiz.q: A die is thrown. E = {1, 3, 5} (odd) and F = {1, 2, 3}. Are E and F independent?
options: No, since P(E ∩ F) = 1/3 but P(E)P(F) = 1/4
Yes, since both have probability 1/2
Yes, since they overlap
No, since they are mutually exclusive
quiz.explain: E ∩ F = {1, 3}, probability 1/3, which is not (1/2)(1/2).
steps: Answer: No, since P(E ∩ F) = 1/3 but P(E)P(F) = 1/4

quiz.q: Which statement is true for events A and B with P(A), P(B) > 0?
options: If they are mutually exclusive, they are not independent
If they are independent, they are mutually exclusive
Independent events cannot happen together
Mutually exclusive events always have P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
quiz.explain: Mutually exclusive gives P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B).
steps: Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) > 0 when both are positive
Both cannot hold, so mutually exclusive events are not independent
Answer: If they are mutually exclusive, they are not independent

quiz.q: A card is drawn from 52. E = 'spade', F = 'ace'. What is P(E ∩ F)?
quiz.explain: Only the ace of spades: 1/52, which equals (1/4)(1/13), so E and F are independent.

quiz.q: For mutual independence of E, F and G, which extra condition is needed besides pairwise independence?
options: P(E ∪ F ∪ G) = 1
P(E) = P(F) = P(G)
E, F, G are mutually exclusive
P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F)P(G)
quiz.explain: Mutual independence needs all three pairwise products and the triple product.
steps: Pairwise: P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), P(F ∩ G) = P(F)P(G), P(E ∩ G) = P(E)P(G)
Mutual independence also needs the triple product rule

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If A and B are independent, then P(A|B) = P(A).
Reason (R): P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = P(A)P(B)/P(B).
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Substituting the independence condition in the definition gives P(A|B) = P(A).
steps: R: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = P(A)P(B)/P(B) = P(A) — true
So A follows directly from R
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the two definitions of independence

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Independent and mutually exclusive sound the same. Are they?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Independent means one doesn't change the other's chance, so P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Mutually exclusive means they can't happen together!
teach.nudge: What is P(A ∩ B) for independent events, and for mutually exclusive ones?

revise.summary: E and F are independent when P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), i.e. knowing F does not change P(E). Independent events are not the same as mutually exclusive events.
focus: Test independence by comparing P(E ∩ F) and P(E)P(F)
Use independence to find P(A ∩ B) and P(A ∪ B)
Know the conditions for three events
remember: Independent ⇔ P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F) ⇔ P(E|F) = P(E)
Mutual independence of three needs pairwise and triple product rules
traps: Independent does not mean mutually exclusive
Equal probabilities do not prove independence
Pairwise independence is not enough for mutual independence

learn.hook: Three bowlers each have a small chance of taking a wicket this over. What is the chance at least one of them does? Flip the question: find the chance none does.
points: If E and F are independent, so are E and F′, E′ and F, and E′ and F′.
P(E′ ∩ F′) = P(E′)P(F′) = (1 − P(E))(1 − P(F)) for independent E, F.
P(at least one of E, F, G) = 1 − P(none) = 1 − P(E′)P(F′)P(G′) for independent events.
With replacement, successive draws are independent; multiply the same probabilities.
To test independence, compare P(E ∩ F) with P(E)P(F).

example.q: Probabilities that A, B and C hit a target are 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4, independently. Find P(at least one hits).

learn.reallife: Disaster managers estimate the chance that at least one of several independent warning systems works, using 1 − P(all fail).

items.q: P(at least one head in 3 tosses)
A solves with 1/2, B with 1/3: P(at least one solves)
P(at least one six in 2 throws of a die)

games.title: Find P(at least one) for independent events

quiz.q: A coin is tossed 3 times. What is P(at least one head)?
quiz.explain: P(no head) = (1/2)³ = 1/8, so P(at least one) = 7/8.

quiz.q: A solves a problem with probability 1/2 and B with 1/3, independently. What is P(the problem is solved)?
quiz.explain: P(neither) = (1/2)(2/3) = 1/3, so P(solved) = 2/3.

quiz.q: P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4, independent. What is P(A ∩ B′)?
quiz.explain: A and B′ are independent: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18.

quiz.q: Two cards are drawn with replacement from 52. What is P(both kings)?
quiz.explain: With replacement the draws are independent: (1/13)(1/13) = 1/169.

quiz.q: A die is thrown twice. What is P(at least one six)?
quiz.explain: P(no six) = (5/6)² = 25/36, so the answer is 11/36.

quiz.q: If E and F are independent with P(E) = 0.2 and P(F) = 0.5, what is P(E′ ∩ F′)?
steps: E, F independent ⇒ E′, F′ independent

quiz.q: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3 and P(A′ ∪ B′) = 5/6. Are A and B independent?
options: Yes, since P(A ∩ B) = 1/6 = P(A)P(B)
No, since P(A ∩ B) = 5/6
No, since P(A) ≠ P(B)
Yes, since P(A′ ∪ B′) < 1
quiz.explain: By De Morgan, A′ ∪ B′ = (A ∩ B)′, so P(A ∩ B) = 1 − 5/6 = 1/6, which equals (1/2)(1/3).
steps: Answer: Yes, since P(A ∩ B) = 1/6 = P(A)P(B)
quiz.mistake: Forgets De Morgan's law A′ ∪ B′ = (A ∩ B)′

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): If A and B are independent, then A′ and B′ are independent.
Reason (R): P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B) = (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)) when A, B are independent.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 1 − P(A) − P(B) + P(A)P(B) factorises as P(A′)P(B′), which is exactly the independence of A′ and B′.
steps: This factorises as (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)) = P(A′)P(B′) — so R is true
P(A′ ∩ B′) = P(A′)P(B′) is exactly independence of A′ and B′
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks complements of independent events are dependent

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the fastest way to find the chance that at least one thing happens?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Find P(none) by multiplying the complements, then 1 minus that. At least one, at lightning speed!
teach.nudge: Instead of adding cases, which single event do you subtract from 1?

revise.summary: If E and F are independent, so are their complements. 'At least one' is easiest as 1 − P(none), multiplying the complement probabilities for independent events.
focus: Use 1 − P(none) for 'at least one'
Find P(A ∩ B′) and P(A′ ∩ B′) for independent events
Use De Morgan to test independence
traps: Don't add probabilities for 'at least one'
P(E′ ∩ F′) is not 1 − P(E)P(F)
Use P(B′), not P(B), in P(A ∩ B′)

learn.hook: A red ball comes out, but which bag did it come from? Bayes' theorem runs probability backwards: from the result to the cause.
points: E₁, E₂, …, Eₙ form a partition of S if they are pairwise disjoint, together make up S, and each has non-zero probability.
Theorem of total probability: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ) P(A|Eᵢ).
Bayes' theorem: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ) P(A|Eᵢ) / Σⱼ P(Eⱼ) P(A|Eⱼ).
Proof idea: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ ∩ A)/P(A); write the top with the multiplication theorem and the bottom with total probability.
The Eᵢ are hypotheses; P(Eᵢ) are prior probabilities and P(Eᵢ|A) are posterior probabilities (after A is observed).

example.q: Bag I has 3 red and 4 black balls; bag II has 5 red and 6 black. A bag is chosen at random and a ball drawn is red. Find P(it came from bag II).

learn.reallife: Many email spam filters use Bayes' theorem: given that certain words appear, what is the chance that the message is spam?

games.title: Applying Bayes' theorem
items: Identify the hypotheses E₁, E₂, … and their priors
Divide the required P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) by P(A)

quiz.q: Bag I has 3 red, 4 black; bag II has 5 red, 6 black. A bag is chosen at random and a red ball is drawn. What is P(bag II | red)?
quiz.mistake: Gives P(red | bag II) instead of P(bag II | red)

quiz.q: Bag A has 2 red and 3 white balls; bag B has 4 red and 1 white. A bag is chosen at random and one ball is drawn. What is P(red)?
quiz.mistake: Adds the bag probabilities without the 1/2 weights

quiz.q: For the same bags, given the ball is red, what is P(it came from bag A)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the prior 1/2 as the answer

quiz.q: Which conditions make E₁, E₂, E₃ a partition of S?
options: Each has probability 1/3
They are independent
They overlap and cover S
Pairwise disjoint, union is S, each with non-zero probability
quiz.explain: A partition splits S into non-overlapping parts that cover it, with positive probabilities.
steps: Partition: no two of E₁, E₂, E₃ overlap
Together they make up S, and each has non-zero probability
They need not be equally likely or independent
Answer: Pairwise disjoint, union is S, each with non-zero probability
quiz.mistake: Thinks the parts must be equally likely

quiz.q: In Bayes' theorem, the probability P(Eᵢ|A) is called the
options: posterior probability
prior probability
total probability
joint probability
quiz.explain: It is the updated probability after A is observed.

quiz.q: Bayes' theorem is derived by combining the definition of conditional probability with
options: only the addition rule
independence of the events
the multiplication theorem and the theorem of total probability
the binomial theorem
quiz.explain: P(Eᵢ ∩ A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) on top; P(A) by total probability below.
steps: Answer: the multiplication theorem and the theorem of total probability

quiz.q: Two bags are equally likely. Bag I: P(red) = 1/4; bag II: P(red) = 3/4. A red ball is drawn. What is P(bag II | red)?

Assertion (A): In the theorem of total probability, the events Eᵢ must form a partition of S.
Reason (R): Then A is the disjoint union of the events A ∩ Eᵢ.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because A = ∪(A ∩ Eᵢ) with disjoint pieces, P(A) = Σ P(A ∩ Eᵢ) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ). R is the reason.
steps: R: if the Eᵢ form a partition, A = (A ∩ E₁) ∪ (A ∩ E₂) ∪ …, with disjoint pieces — true
So P(A) = Σ P(A ∩ Eᵢ) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ)
That is why a partition is required: R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does Bayes' theorem do, and how do I use it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Bayes runs backwards from result to cause: the chosen path's P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) divided by the total P(A)!
teach.nudge: What goes in the denominator of Bayes' formula?

revise.summary: If E₁, …, Eₙ partition S, then P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) (total probability). Bayes' theorem reverses the condition: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ)/Σ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ).
focus: Find P(A) by total probability
Find a posterior probability with Bayes' theorem
Know the meaning of partition, prior and posterior
remember: Partition: disjoint, union S, each P(Eᵢ) > 0
traps: Don't give P(A|Eᵢ) when P(Eᵢ|A) is asked
Weight each bag or group by its prior
Don't report the prior as the answer

learn.hook: A test is 99% accurate, yet a positive result may still mean only about a 1-in-6 chance of disease. Bayes' theorem explains this surprise.
points: Factories: P(machine | defective) uses each machine's output share and defect rate.
Medical tests: the disease's rarity (prior) matters as much as test accuracy.
Truth-telling: P(event really happened | reported) depends on the event's chance and the reporter's honesty.
Insurance and groups: weight each group by its share of the population.
Random variables, probability distributions, mean, variance and the binomial distribution are not in the current CBSE syllabus.

example.q: Machines A, B, C make 25%, 35% and 40% of bolts, with 5%, 4% and 2% defective. A bolt is defective. Find P(it was made by B).

learn.reallife: During health screenings, doctors explain that a positive result for a rare condition needs a second confirmatory test, exactly because Bayes' theorem lowers the posterior probability.

games.title: Medical test with Bayes
items: Likelihoods: P(+ | disease) = 0.99, P(+ | no disease) = 0.005

games.title: Bayes intuition
items: A very accurate test always means a positive result is almost certainly correct.
For rare conditions, false positives can outnumber true positives.
In Bayes problems, the priors must add to 1.
P(A|B) and P(B|A) are usually equal.
Bayes' theorem connects them; they differ in general.
A machine with a small share of output can still be a likely source of defects if its defect rate is high.
The posterior depends on share × defect rate.
Binomial distribution is part of the current CBSE Class XII syllabus.
It has been removed from the rationalised syllabus.

quiz.q: Machines A, B, C produce 25%, 35%, 40% of bolts with 5%, 4%, 2% defective. A bolt is defective. What is P(made by B)?
quiz.mistake: Uses B's share 35% as the answer

quiz.q: For the same machines, what is P(made by C | defective)?
A man tells the truth 3 out of 4 times. He throws a die and reports a six. What is P(it is actually a six)?
0.1% of people have a disease. A test detects it 99% of the time and gives a false positive 0.5% of the time. What is P(disease | positive)?
quiz.mistake: Assumes the posterior equals the test's accuracy

quiz.q: An insurer has 2000 scooter, 4000 car and 6000 truck drivers with accident probabilities 0.01, 0.03 and 0.15. An insured person has an accident. What is P(scooter driver)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the scooter share 1/6 as the answer

quiz.q: For the same insurer, what is P(truck driver | accident)?
quiz.explain: Using the scaled weights 0.01, 0.06, 0.45: 0.45/0.52 = 45/52.

quiz.q: In a class, 40% are girls and 60% are boys. 25% of girls and 10% of boys got an A grade. A student with an A is picked. What is P(the student is a girl)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the prior 40% as the answer

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Even a 99% accurate test can give a low P(disease | positive) for a rare disease.
Reason (R): When the prior is very small, false positives from the large healthy group can outnumber true positives.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: In the 0.1% example, true positives are 0.00099 while false positives are 0.004995, about five times more. That gives a posterior near 0.165.
steps: False positives are about 5 times the true positives, so P(disease | positive) ≈ 0.165
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: 'A test is 99% accurate and I tested positive. Am I 99% likely to be sick?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Not necessarily! If the disease is rare, false positives from healthy people pile up, and Bayes' theorem gives a much lower chance!
teach.nudge: What role does how rare the disease is play?

revise.summary: Bayes' theorem answers 'which source caused it' questions for factories, tests, truth-tellers and insurance groups. Weight each source by its share, then divide by the total probability.
focus: Set up priors and likelihoods from a word problem
Compute the posterior for one source
Explain why rare-disease tests can mislead
remember: Rare events: false positives from the large group can outnumber true positives
traps: Don't use a machine's output share as the answer
Don't assume P(disease | positive) equals test accuracy
Scale percentages consistently before dividing
